AsyncLocalStorage (Node's async_hooks) lets you stash a value, like a request id, at the top of a request and read it anywhere down the async call chain without passing it through every function. The overhead is usually small next to real I/O, but it is not free, and it has historically cost more in hot paths with lots of promises, so measure on our own load if it matters. It would fit the requestId problem you just raised, since the logger and error handler could read the id from the store. Middleware runs before routing and caching on every request, so Next defaults it to the edge runtime: it starts fast, runs close to the user, and can cheaply redirect or rewrite. Newer Next versions let middleware opt into the Node runtime, but I'd check which version we're on before relying on that. `using` declares a resource that is disposed automatically when the scope exits: the object gets a `[Symbol.dispose]()` method and the runtime calls it, even on throw or early return. `await using` does the same with `Symbol.asyncDispose`, and multiple resources are disposed in reverse order. It needs TS 5.2 or later plus a runtime that has the symbols (or a polyfill), so it depends on our Node version and tsconfig lib settings. Action: Answer only for now; I can check our TS version, tsconfig target/lib and Node version to tell you whether we could use it here.

They're different things. HTTP/1.1 keep-alive only reuses the TCP connection, but requests on it still go one at a time, so a slow response blocks the ones behind it (browsers work around that by opening several connections). HTTP/2 multiplexes many concurrent request/response streams as interleaved frames on a single connection, plus header compression. It still has TCP-level head-of-line blocking if a packet is lost, which is what HTTP/3 over QUIC addresses. Action: None needed; I can check whether staging actually serves h2 if that's useful for the standup.

JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) only keeps plain JSON: Dates become strings, Map and Set become empty objects, undefined and functions vanish, and cycles throw. structuredClone keeps Dates, Maps, Sets, typed arrays and handles cycles, but it can't clone functions or DOM nodes, and class instances lose their prototype. So the reviewer is right to flag it unless the data is plain JSON. Action: If you tell me which PR it is, I'll find the flagged line and say whether it's safe or needs structuredClone.
